source_refs.note: Topic 4.8, printed pages 119-124: nucleotides, bases, the phosphodiester bond, ATP and NAD, the Watson and Crick model, genes, the three RNAs and the central dogma.

blocks.text: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotide units. There are two main types, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA). DNA is found mainly in chromosomes, with small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts; RNA is found in the nucleolus, ribosomes and cytosol. A nucleotide is made of a nucleoside and phosphoric acid, and a nucleoside is made of a nitrogenous base and a pentose sugar.

blocks.alt: Flow chart: Nucleic acid (a column of repeating coloured units) -> Nucleotide -> Nucleoside and Phosphoric acid; Nucleoside -> Nitrogen base and Pentose sugar.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.39: Components of nucleic acids (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.39).

items: Pentose sugars: RNA contains ribose and DNA contains deoxyribose as their pentoses.

Nitrogenous bases: there are two types in nucleic acids, pyrimidine bases and purine bases. Pyrimidine is a single-ringed base; there are three pyrimidine bases in nucleic acids: cytosine (C) in both DNA and RNA, thymine (T) only in DNA, and uracil (U) only in RNA. Purine is a double-ringed base; both DNA and RNA contain the two purine bases adenine (A) and guanine (G). One nitrogenous base attaches to carbon 1 of the pentose sugar and makes a nucleoside.

Phosphoric acid: a nucleoside develops an ester linkage with a phosphoric acid and becomes a nucleotide; in this ester linkage the phosphoric acid is linked to C-5 of the pentose sugar. The backbone of nucleic acids is made of sugars and phosphates.

blocks.alt: A shaded vertical backbone of alternating phosphates (P) and pentose sugar rings; from each sugar a base (single or double ring) sticks out to the right. Labels: Backbone, Bases.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.40: Sugar-phosphate backbone of nucleic acids (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.40).

blocks.alt: Five nucleotides, each a pentose ring (carbons 1 to 5, ring O) with P on carbon 5 and a base on carbon 1. Pyrimidines (one six-membered ring): cytosine (NH2, N, O), thymine (CH3, O, NH, O) and uracil (O, NH, O). Purines (a six-membered ring fused along an edge to a five-membered ring): adenine (NH2) and guanine (O, NH, NH2).
blocks.caption: Figure 4.41: Nucleotides of RNA and DNA (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.41).

blocks.text: In one nucleotide the phosphoric acid has an ester linkage at C-5 of the pentose sugar. This phosphoric acid develops another ester linkage at C-3 of the pentose sugar of another nucleotide. In this way each phosphoric acid has two ester linkages with two pentose sugars, one at C-5 and the other at C-3; these two ester linkages are the phosphodiester linkage, which joins two nucleotides. The nucleotides of RNA are ribonucleotides and those of DNA are deoxyribonucleotides; nucleotides are named after their nitrogenous base.

blocks.alt: Two nucleotides: the upper with cytosine on its sugar and P-O on carbon 5; carbon 3 of its sugar is joined through O-P(=O)(O)-O to carbon 5 of the lower sugar, which carries adenine. The O-P-O link is bracketed and labelled Phosphodiester linkage.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.42: A dinucleotide (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.42).

blocks.title: ATP and NAD
blocks.text: Nucleotides also play other critical roles in the life of the cell. ATP is a triphosphate nucleotide of adenine: three phosphate groups attached to one ribose sugar. ATP is the energy currency of the cell; it provides energy by successively detaching two phosphate groups, changing to ADP and then AMP. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) is a coenzyme that acts as a hydrogen acceptor in the oxidation-reduction reactions of the cell.

blocks.alt: Left, Adenosine Triphosphate: HO-P-O-P-O-P-O (three phosphate groups) joined to carbon 5 of ribose, with adenine on carbon 1. Right, Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide: nicotinamide ring on a ribose, joined through two phosphates to a second ribose carrying adenine. Labels: Phosphate groups, Ribose, Adenine, Nicotinamide.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.43: ATP and NAD (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.43).

blocks.text: Nucleotides join through phosphodiester linkages to form long polynucleotide chains. In a polynucleotide chain the phosphate group at the 5' end and the OH group at the 3' end are always free. RNA is made of a single polynucleotide chain; DNA is a double helix made of two polynucleotide chains.

Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins studied the molecular architecture of DNA. James D. Watson and Francis Crick put forward the model of DNA in 1953; the observations of Chargaff were also of basic importance in working out the structure.

blocks.title: Before Watson and Crick
blocks.text: In 1950 Linus Pauling concluded that DNA is a fibrous substance and that the fibre is coiled into a helix. In 1951 Erwin Chargaff provided informative data showing that adenine and thymine are equal in ratio in DNA, and so are guanine and cytosine.
The Watson and Crick model of DNA suggests the following points.

items: DNA is made of two polynucleotide chains, or strands.
The two strands are coiled around each other to make a double helix.
The double helix is like a ladder. Its poles are made of sugars and phosphate groups; its rungs are made of pairs of nitrogenous bases.
Each base pair (rung) is made of one purine (A or G) and one pyrimidine (C or T).
The two strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between their bases.

Adenine in one chain makes hydrogen bonds with thymine in the second chain, or vice versa; guanine in one chain makes hydrogen bonds with cytosine in the second, or vice versa. There are two hydrogen bonds between an A-T pair and three between a G-C pair.
The two strands do not run in the same direction with respect to their phosphodiester linkages; they are antiparallel to each other.

blocks.alt: (a) A double helix 2 nm wide; base-pair rungs join the two strands; one full turn is 3.4 nm and base pairs are 0.34 nm apart; minor and major grooves labelled. (b) Two antiparallel strands of sugars and phosphates (P) with paired bases C-G, A-T, C-G, G-C joined by dashed hydrogen bonds (two for A-T, three for G-C). Each strand starts with a 5' phosphate and ends at a 3' sugar.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.44: (a) Watson and Crick model of DNA, (b) The detailed structure of DNA (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.44).

blocks.text: DNA is the fundamental part of chromosomes and so lies inside the nucleus in eukaryotes. As prokaryotes have no distinct nucleus, their DNA is in the cytoplasm. In viruses, DNA is the core molecule, covered by a protein coat. DNA is the hereditary material of all organisms except some viruses. It contains the "program" that ultimately directs all cellular activities, in the form of genes. A gene is a sequence of DNA nucleotides that codes for the formation of a polypeptide. When a gene is turned "on", the sequence of DNA nucleotides is transcribed into RNA and then translated into specific proteins. In this way DNA controls the properties and activities of a cell.

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: In eukaryotes a small amount (about 2 percent) of DNA is also present in mitochondria and chloroplasts. In the chromosome of the bacterium E. coli each strand of DNA contains about 5 million bases in a particular linear order, with genes each consisting of several hundred bases.

RNA is composed of ribonucleotides. It is synthesised by joining ribonucleotides in front of the deoxyribonucleotides of DNA in the process of transcription. All living cells contain three types of RNA.

items: Messenger RNA (mRNA) consists of a single strand of ribonucleotides whose sequence is complementary to the sequence of nucleotides of one of the strands of DNA. It is about 3 to 4 percent of the total RNA in the cell. It carries the genetic message of DNA to the ribosomes to form a particular protein.

Transfer RNA (tRNA) is comparatively small, a helical structure whose molecule resembles a clover leaf. It is 10 to 15 percent of the total RNA. tRNAs transport amino acids to the ribosome and mRNA in protein synthesis.

Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is synthesised by the DNA of the nucleoli. After its synthesis it is joined with ribosomal protein and ribosomes are formed. It is about 80 percent of the total RNA and acts as the machinery for protein synthesis in ribosomes.

blocks.alt: A single coiled strand: a blue sugar-phosphate backbone with coloured nitrogenous bases projecting from it. Labels: Sugar-Phosphate backbone, Nitrogenous bases.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.45: A model of RNA structure (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.45).

blocks.text: All organisms use the same basic mechanism of reading and expressing genes, often referred to as the central dogma. The first step is the transfer of information from DNA to RNA, which occurs when an RNA copy of a gene is produced; this process is transcription. The second step is the transfer of information from RNA to protein, which occurs when the information in the RNA is used to direct the synthesis of a protein; this process is translation. In this way DNA controls the properties and activities of a cell.

blocks.alt: DNA (a double helix) -> arrow labelled Transcription (DNA -> RNA) -> RNA (a single strand with bases) -> arrow labelled Translation (RNA -> Protein) -> Protein (a chain of beads).
